# Lahmu — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

The internet spells **Lahmu** more ways than one, and only one of them is the name the sources wrote. This is the register's ruling — canonical, fallback, contested, and false, each in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Lahmu
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒌓𒈬
- **Pantheon:** Mesopotamian
- **Convention:** Assyriological transliteration — š, ṣ, ṭ, ḫ as the sign lists require
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 270 of 542

## The Canonical Form

The attested form is **𒀭𒌓𒈬**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Lahmu**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form Assyriological transliteration — š, ṣ, ṭ, ḫ as the sign lists require demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *lahmu* differs from the canonical **Lahmu** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — Assyriological transliteration — š, ṣ, ṭ, ḫ as the sign lists require — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Lahmu**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

The oldest writing system on earth encodes its gods in wedge marks on clay, and its consonant system outruns the Latin alphabet: š is a hushing sibilant, ṣ and ṭ are emphatics produced deep in the mouth, ḫ is a rasp English lost centuries ago. When nineteenth-century decipherers built the transliteration conventions Assyriology still uses, they chose diacritics precisely so that none of those distinctions would be flattened. This register honors the same choice for the same reason: the tablets distinguish; so do we.

## What the Address Bar Allows

IDNA 2008 permits the letters these restorations use — macrons, acutes, underdots, thorn, ogonek, the lot — and the DNS carries them as punycode (`xn--` labels). Two honest constraints remain. First, **registrar inventory**: the protocol permits a character; the registrar's stock decides whether the exact domain can be bought today. Second, **combined marks**: forms like *Apṓllōn* (acute stacked on a macron) are philologically ideal yet effectively untypeable on phones and unsupported across much of the registration system.

That is why the rulebook keeps a fallback hierarchy — full restoration first, then the circumflex when the source carries one, then the macron-only academic standard, then an attested variant, and only as a last resort the plain ASCII form. **Every step down the ladder is still defensible; nothing on the ladder is a wrong mark.** A fallback is a choice among attested forms. A false form is not on the ladder at all.

## Where the Name Stood First

Archaeological evidence for Lahmu consists chiefly of protective figurines, glazed brick reliefs, and seal impressions. Neo-Assyrian palace gateways, notably at Khorsabad and Nineveh, were flanked by apotropaic colossi whose iconography overlaps with the lahmu type. Clay figurines buried in foundation deposits and door sockets invoke his protective function. Cuneiform copies of the Enuma Elish from Nineveh and Babylon preserve his cosmogonic role. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Verdict

The register rules for **Lahmu**, and the ruling is checkable: every mark sourced, every violation stated, every borderline form given its honest standing. *lahmu* carries the name freely — it differs only in display, and the register says so without reservation. Anything else in circulation has its origin and its failure recorded above. That is the whole of the law on this name — and the temple at [/lahmu/](/lahmu/) enforces it.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 7 cited sources — Enuma Elish, Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia, CAD (Chicago Assyrian Dictionary), s.v. lahmu / lahāmu.
